opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think they're going to develop pretty differently, and on different timelines.

On the consumer side, the big constraint is cost and latency. You're serving hundreds of millions of people, many of them on free tiers, so every token matters. A lot of the work there is making inference cheap and fast enough that you can give people a really good experience: snappy voice interaction, real-time responses, maybe running smaller models on device. Consumers are also less tolerant of waiting. If something takes thirty seconds, people leave. So I think consumer AI will be shaped heavily by systems and efficiency work: better kernels, quantization, architectures that handle long context cheaply, things like that. The use cases will be companionship, search-like tasks, creative tools, education. Things where the model is a conversational partner more than a worker.

Enterprise and professional agents are a different beast. There the value of getting a task right is much higher. If an agent can do a few hours of a software engineer's work or a financial analyst's work, people are happy to wait, and happy to pay a lot more per task. So you can spend way more inference compute: longer reasoning, many tool calls, checking its own work, running tests. Coding is the clearest example right now, because you have a fast feedback loop. You can run the code and see if it works. I think we'll see that spread to other domains where you can build good verification and environments.

The hard parts for enterprise are less about raw model capability and more about reliability, integration, and context. The agent needs to understand your codebase, your internal docs, your workflows, and it needs to fail gracefully. That's where long context and memory become really important, and also a lot of unglamorous engineering.

So my rough picture is: consumer is a scale and efficiency game, enterprise is a reliability and depth game. Interestingly, the inference efficiency work helps both. Cheaper tokens make consumer products viable, and they also let agents think longer for the same price. That's a big part of why I'm excited about the systems side. Every time we make inference a few times cheaper, a whole new set of applications opens up.

r001.rationale: It discusses enterprise and professional agents, but does not predict that agents will be the main AI use case in those settings.

r002.rationale: It mentions real-time voice interaction and responses, but makes no claim about real-time video generation substantially changing consumer AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, actually, because the two are shaped by really different constraints, and those constraints end up dictating what the models and the systems underneath them need to look like.

On the consumer side, the dominant thing is latency and cost. If you're building something for hundreds of millions of people, every token you generate has a price, and the user is sitting there waiting. So you want models that feel instant, that are cheap enough to run at massive scale, and that are good at the kinds of things people actually do day to day: ask a question, draft a message, summarize something, maybe talk to it with voice. A lot of that is pushing toward smaller, more efficient models, better inference systems, things like speculative decoding, better attention kernels, better memory management on the serving side. The quality bar is high but the task horizon is short. You're not asking the model to go away for an hour and come back.

The enterprise and professional agent side is almost the inverse. There the task horizon is long. You want the model to take a vague instruction, go run code, read documents, call tools, check its own work, and come back with something done. The economics are different too. If an agent saves an engineer a day of work, you can afford to spend a lot of compute on it. So the pressure is less on per-token cost and more on reliability, on long context, on the model being able to maintain state and recover from mistakes over thousands of steps. That pushes you toward bigger models, more test-time compute, and architectures that handle very long sequences well, which is obviously something I care about from the attention and state space side.

What's interesting is that they're converging in one direction and diverging in another. They converge on the systems layer, because whether you're serving a chatbot or an agent, you need to decode tokens fast and handle long contexts without blowing up memory. Those are the same kernels, the same hardware problems. But they diverge in how you'd design the product and even how you'd train the model. For consumer you optimize for breadth and vibes and speed. For enterprise agents you optimize for correctness on narrow, high-value workflows, and you're willing to trade speed for that.

My guess is consumer apps will adopt agentic behavior more slowly than people expect, because the trust and latency requirements are brutal. Most people don't want to wait five minutes for their phone to do something. But enterprise agents will keep moving fast, because the people using them are already comfortable waiting on a long job if the result is good. And then over the next few years the efficiency work, the stuff that makes inference ten times cheaper, is what lets those agentic capabilities leak back into consumer products. So the research that matters for both ends up being the same: make the models handle long contexts, make generation fast, make it cheap. The products just sit at different points on that curve.

r001.rationale: The response predicts enterprise agents will keep moving fast, but does not say they will be the main AI use case in professional or enterprise settings.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention real-time video generation or predict that it will substantially change consumer AI.

astra-6.text:
I think the professional use cases have a clearer path, because you can attach a value to the work. If an agent helps a software engineer finish a task faster, or automates part of a workflow, you can measure whether it’s useful and how much you’re willing to pay for it. You also have a person there who can check the output, so the system can be valuable before it’s fully autonomous.

Consumer applications feel more open-ended to me. What makes someone come back every day? It might be usefulness, but it could also be entertainment or connection. Those are harder to capture with a benchmark. A model getting better at coding doesn’t necessarily tell you what the next great consumer product will look like.

So I’d expect more predictable progress in professional tools, and more experimentation on the consumer side. There, the product experience and understanding what people actually want may matter just as much as the underlying model.

r001.rationale: The response says professional tools have a clearer path and gives agent examples, but it does not predict that agents will be the main professional or enterprise AI use case.

r002.rationale: The response discusses consumer applications generally and makes no prediction about real-time video generation changing the consumer AI landscape.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the professional use cases have a clearer feedback loop. If an agent helps you write code or analyze data, you can often check whether the result is correct and measure how much time it saves. That makes it easier to improve the product and figure out what people will pay for.

On the consumer side, I think there’s more uncertainty about what the product should look like. A general assistant is useful, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you what will make someone come back every day. It could be education, entertainment, or something much more personalized. My guess is that the successful applications will require as much experimentation with the user experience as with the models themselves.

r001.rationale: The response says professional agent use cases have clearer feedback loops, but does not predict that agents will be the main AI use case in professional or enterprise settings.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty and experimentation in consumer applications, but does not mention real-time video generation or predict its impact.
